title: Job Remembers His Better Days
overview: Job looks back with longing on the years when he felt close to God, had his family around him, and was respected for his fairness and care for people in need.

parts.label: When God felt near (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Job remembers a time when God's favor felt like a lamp lighting his way through dark places, and like a close friend's presence in his home. Paths flowing with cream and rocks pouring out olive oil are pictures of overflowing plenty, since milk and oil were the wealth of a herding and farming household.

parts.label: Honored at the city gate (vv. 7-11)
parts.note: The city gate was where elders gathered to judge cases and settle public matters, and Job had a seat of honor there. Young men stepping back, old men standing, and leaders covering their mouths were customary signs of deep respect: everyone waited to hear what he would say.

parts.label: Defender of the helpless (vv. 12-17)
parts.note: Job explains why people praised him: he stood up for orphans, widows, the disabled, the dying and outsiders, and broke the power of those who preyed on them. Many readers hear this as a reply to the charge in chapter 22 that Job mistreated widows and orphans, though Job does not name his accuser here.

parts.label: Expecting a long, secure life (vv. 18-20)
parts.note: Job assumed he would die old and at home, like a well watered tree that never dries out, with his strength always renewed like a fresh bow. The word translated "sand" might instead mean the legendary phoenix bird, a symbol of long life, and scholars are not sure which is meant.

parts.label: Words like welcome rain (vv. 21-25)
parts.note: People waited for Job's advice the way dry fields wait for spring rain, and once he spoke no one argued. The meaning of verse 24 is uncertain: it may say people could hardly believe he smiled at them, or that his smile cheered those who had lost hope.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Job's account of his own goodness here is a fair and honest defense, since God later says Job spoke rightly, or whether it shows a pride that the rest of the book gently corrects.
think: When life takes a turn for the worse, does remembering better days tend to help you, or make the present harder to bear?
